comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C1, C48, C49, C100, C101 regarding cone density-acuity correlation. Both evaluations find the evidence convincing and well-supported with appropriate statistical analysis (r²=0.45, p=0.005 for dominant eyes). Peer reviewers emphasize the work is 'rigorously conducted.'

Strong agreement on claims C2, C46, C102 regarding sub-Nyquist resolution. Both evaluations support that all participants exceeded the Nyquist limit at 788 nm. OpenEval additionally addresses C47 (wavelength-dependent differences) not explicitly mentioned in peer evaluation. Peer reviewers note improvements from previous version regarding Nyquist limit description.

Perfect agreement on claims C3, C69, C70, C117 regarding drift length-acuity correlation. Both evaluations affirm the correlation is solid and statistically supported. OpenEval notes r² values indicate drift explains only ~25-29% of variance, suggesting other factors are important.

Strong agreement on claims C5, C72, C73, C76, C122, C123, C151 regarding directional drift toward CDC. Both evaluations describe this as a central, important finding with convincing evidence. OpenEval includes additional claims C74, C75 not explicitly mentioned in peer evaluation. Peer reviewers emphasize this challenges the view of drift as random and is 'state-of-the-art.'

Perfect agreement on claim C71 regarding lack of correlation between drift length and cone density. Both evaluations accept this null finding as important evidence that drift is not simply scaled to cone density, supporting controlled behavior interpretation.

Perfect agreement on claims C58, C59 regarding fixational behavior and microsaccade suppression. Both evaluations accept these observations without challenge as part of comprehensive eye movement characterization.

Perfect agreement on claims C143-C150 regarding study population and experimental design. Both evaluations praise the sample size (20 subjects) and methodology. Peer reviewers emphasize this is 'a real tour-de-force' given the challenging nature of AO psychophysics experiments.

Perfect agreement on claims C60-C68 regarding drift characterization measurements. Both evaluations accept these measurements as reliable and well-analyzed using state-of-the-art technology. Peer reviewers note data analysis improvements after first review round.

Strong agreement on claims C77, C78, C81, C82, C83 regarding differential directionality toward CDC versus PRL/PCD. Both evaluations affirm this comparative finding. OpenEval additionally addresses C139, C140 which peer reviewers discuss separately in R14.

Strong agreement on claims C84-C89 regarding onset distance, drift length correlations, and sampling gain. Both evaluations accept the quantitative analyses as rigorous. OpenEval provides detailed statistical values while peer reviewers emphasize improved statistical testing in revised version.

Partial agreement on claims C79, C80 regarding ISOA reduction. Both evaluations support this finding. However, peer R12 also addresses claims C84-C89 which OpenEval evaluates separately in R7, showing some grouping differences between evaluations.

Strong agreement on claims C55, C56, C57 regarding mismatch between cone density differences and acuity differences between fellow eyes. Both evaluations accept the logic and calculations. Peer R8 additionally addresses C50, C51 which OpenEval evaluates separately in R8.

Partial agreement on claims C50, C51 regarding acuity differences between fellow eyes. Both evaluations support these findings. OpenEval additionally addresses C52, C53, C54 regarding cone density comparisons and correlations, while peer R8 also includes C55, C56, C57 which OpenEval evaluates separately in R5.

Partial agreement on claims C41, C42 regarding basic measurements. Both evaluations accept these as foundational data. OpenEval R11 addresses C43, C44, C45 (cone density measurements) which peer reviewers evaluate in R7, while peer R6 also addresses C93 which OpenEval evaluates in R16.

Strong agreement on claims C43, C44, C45 regarding cone density measurements. Both evaluations accept these anatomical measurements as part of rigorous methodology using state-of-the-art AOSLO technology without challenge.

Partial overlap on claims C128, C5 regarding temporal development of directionality and adaptive control. Both evaluations support controlled drift behavior. OpenEval R17 focuses on temporal aspects and feedback mechanisms with C129, while peer R4 provides broader evaluation of directional drift findings.

Partial overlap on claims C139, C140 regarding PRL shifts toward CDC during resolution tasks. Both evaluations support this finding as evidence of task-dependent control. OpenEval R6 groups these with broader CDC directionality claims, while peer R14 treats PRL observations as separate evidence of controlled drift.

Partial overlap on claim C93 regarding acuity measurements. Both evaluations accept these measurements. OpenEval R16 focuses on comparison to literature (Rossi et al., 2007) and wavelength effects with C90-C92, C94, while peer R6 emphasizes overall data quality and methodology.

Partial overlap on claim C94 regarding comparison to previous work. Both evaluations accept wavelength-dependent differences and optical explanations. OpenEval addresses C90-C93 regarding literature comparisons, while peer R16 also includes C47, C103, C104 regarding mechanistic explanations.

Minimal overlap on claim C47 regarding wavelength-dependent differences. OpenEval R2 evaluates this as part of sub-Nyquist resolution findings with photopigment sensitivity explanation, while peer R16 addresses it alongside optical factors C103, C104 without challenging the explanations.

Both address historical context and prior understanding. OpenEval R15 evaluates claims C7, C17, C18, C19 regarding literature gaps and prior knowledge as accurately characterized. Peer R5 evaluates C4, C29 regarding the historical view of drift as random, which the current work challenges. Both accept these contextual claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C97, C95, C96 regarding the dominant role of optical factors over cone density, rating them as UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct testing of varying aberration correction levels. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific interpretive claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C108, C106, C107 regarding sub-Nyquist resolution mechanisms and aliasing, finding them supported by experimental data and cited literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these mechanistic claims about aliasing and prior knowledge.

OpenEval evaluates claims C118, C119, C120 regarding spatial frequency modulation mechanisms, finding them supported by cited modeling work. These mechanistic explanations rely primarily on literature rather than direct experimental evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these theoretical mechanisms.

Peer reviewers evaluate claims C4, C29 regarding the historical view of drift as random, which the current work challenges. This contextual framing is accepted as accurately representing prior understanding. OpenEval addresses related historical context in R15 but with different claim IDs (C7, C17, C18, C19).
